method: Read all 46 outgoing and 5 incoming primary bodies from fox.packet.json in bounded, untruncated batches before consulting initial_survey.json. Paragraph arrays below record the complete retained body coverage, including editorially retained postscript blocks; editorial summaries and footnotes were treated as editorial evidence only.

findings: All 46 assigned outgoing records and all 5 assigned incoming records are included with complete retained paragraph-number coverage.

The strongest correspondence evidence is explicit wording about receipt, reading, crossed letters, forwarding, delays, or exact enclosures; shared entomology, family topics, or chronology alone were not used as receipt evidence.

Incoming 99 matches outgoing 100 on the distinctive microscope gift event. The evidence supports source_event_match/no_whole_note_availability; it does not establish that Darwin read the note, and the archival author need not have been known to him.

Several outgoing letters explicitly refer to unlocated Fox inputs. These references remain unlocated and are not collapsed into incoming 90, 91, 93, 95, or 99 without distinctive evidence; repeated references may represent aliases for the same missing input.

Third-party routes remain distinct in the all-correspondence graph: Fox-to-Holden and Bessy-to-Catherine are not Darwin inputs, while Turner, Catherine, Pulleine, Simpson, and Matthew’s reply to missing Darwin text are in-scope incoming or cross-group edges when explicitly attested.

Explicit crossed-letter statements occur in 46 and 76; 57 also distinguishes a Fox letter received from Darwin's own failed forwarding. These are communication-channel evidence, not license to infer identities for missing letters.
limitations: This review is limited to the bodies and metadata in fox.packet.json plus comparison with initial_survey.json; unlocated letters are described but not reconstructed.
The packet's assigned incoming scope contains 5 records, while the broader project notes 34 eligible incoming bodies; no unassigned incoming body was used here.
Editorial summaries and footnotes were not treated as words Darwin wrote or as proof of what he knew.
